Final report · 17 November 2026 · Netflix US and Canada Q4 2019–Q4 2025 · Five Below FY2018–FY2025

Netflix grew by adding households, not by raising price. Five Below's margin tracked how many stores it opened.

Netflix raised prices six times and kept its customers. US and Canada revenue doubled. Since 2023, most new revenue came from more paying households, mainly through the paid-sharing crackdown. Price rises do seem to cost some members, though the signal is borderline. Five Below's weak years followed its two biggest opening years by store count, not by percent fleet growth. New stores stayed productive. Every result rests on 8 to 24 data points, so each is a lead to test, not proof.

Part A

The answer in plain language

A.1

The questions, and the five numbers that decide them

Netflix: what did US price increases do to memberships, revenue per member and revenue (Q4 2019 to Q4 2024)? Five Below: does the store expansion pace make sense, are new stores as productive as the base, and what did fast-opening years do to comparable sales and margin (FY2018 to FY2025)? Source: problem_description.md

#NumberWhat it means for the decisionLabelSource
1US and Canada quarterly revenue rose from $2,672M (Q4 2019) to $5,339M (Q4 2025), +100%Price rises did not shrink revenue. No price step was followed by a revenue fallmeasuredhandoff §1; chart 01
2Member growth supplied 72% (2023) and 68% (2024) of yearly revenue growth. In 2022, price supplied it all (members −0.7%)Recent growth came from more paying households, not higher prices. Protect member growth before the next price stepmeasured (descriptive arithmetic)followups R2 Q2
3Higher price-per-member growth went with weaker next-quarter member additions: rho [rank correlation] = −0.474, p = 0.064, 16 quartersPrice has a cost. The result is borderline, so it is a warning that needs a proper testmeasuredfollowups R1 Q4
4Each +$1 a month of price per member is worth about $1.08B a year on 89.63M members. It breaks even if about 4.9M members (5.5%) leave. The worst single quarter lost 1.3MPast price steps had a wide safety margin. The margin shrinks if cheaper ad-plan sign-ups pull the average price downmeasured arithmetic; flat membership is assumedfollowups R1 Q1; memo N3
5Five Below's operating margin fell as yearly store openings rose: rho = −0.82, p = 0.033, 6 normal years. By percent fleet growth there is no such link (rho = +0.50)The limit is how many stores teams can open well each year. Cap openings by count, near 150measuredfollowups R1 Q5; memo F2
A.2

Five next steps: test price, save members, earn each store
#ActionCompanyWhySource
1Run a billing-cycle price test: delay the March 2026 increase for a random 5% of members for 60 days and compare cancellationsNetflixTurns the borderline price signal (number 3) into a measured answermemo N4, NF-1
2Offer the $8.99 ad plan to people at the cancel screen, with a random no-offer groupNetflixKeeping a member at $8.99 beats losing a $19.99 membermemo N4, NF-2
3Keep at least 12 months between price stepsNetflixThe negative link in number 3 argues against tighter spacingmemo N3, Track B
4Hold FY2026 at about 150 new stores. Raise the count by about 25 only when the last class of new stores reaches $2.0M first-year salesFive BelowMargin tracked opening count, and management already guides about 150memo F3
5Test an opening-cadence cap (two openings per district manager per quarter) in matched regionsFive BelowChecks whether pace itself, rather than merchandise changes, drives resultsmemo F4, FB-1
What is uncertain. Every effect is an association from 6 to 24 data points, none proven cause. Netflix stopped reporting members after Q4 2024, so 2025 members and price per member cannot be checked. Five Below's FY2025 rebound coincides with a pricing and merchandise reset that the data cannot separate from slower openings.

Tuning history

No Optuna run, so no optimization history. With 8 to 24 rows, a large search would fit noise. The only setting tuned was the penalty strength alpha, over five values (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100). There were no trials and no parameter-importance result. Selected alphas: 0.01 for Netflix, 100 for Five Below. Source: tuning.md.

Selection rule, set before results: lowest error, at most two features (Five Below) or four (Netflix), sensible signs, simpler model on near-ties.

ModelResultWhat it means
Netflix revenueWalk-forward MAE $92.7M, inside the $100M target set before modelingGood at tracking the trend one quarter ahead
Netflix revenue, held-out Q1 2025Predicted $4,705M vs actual $4,617M; residual −$88MOne test point only. The model over-predicted (the handoff text says "underpredicted"; see Part C)
Five Below comps11.07 points, far above the 1.5-point targetNot usable for forecasts. It cannot predict the COVID swings
Five Below margin1.79 points, close to the 1.5-point targetWeak but better than guessing the average
  • The Netflix revenue model is a momentum model. Last quarter's revenue carries it (weight 1.23, p < 0.001). The ARM weight is −72, p = 0.18, because of collinearity.
  • Both Five Below models have negative R²: worse than guessing the average.
  • The Five Below comp model's weight on expansion rate is +7.87 (p = 0.96), so the model card's "higher expansion, lower comps" is not supported by it.

B7

Agent dialogue: 12 questions in two rounds changed four headline claims

The strategy partner questioned the statistician by direct message. None was declined; nothing is still open. Questions as logged in agent_dialogue.md; answers quoted from ml_followups.md.

Round 1 · Q1Netflix §1 levers, §2UCAN end-of-quarter paid memberships at Q4'24: chart exploration/02 shows ~89.6M, but handoff §6 uses 83M. Whi…
Growth-strategy partner askedUCAN end-of-quarter paid memberships at Q4'24: chart exploration/02 shows ~89.6M, but handoff §6 uses 83M. Which is right? Please restate the $1/month ARM → annual revenue arithmetic at the correct base. Also explain the "~$360M/year per $1/month" in handoff §2 and actionability_netflix.csv; at 83M × $1 × 12 I get ~$1.0B, not $360M.
ML statistician answered"Q4'24 UCAN paid members = 89.63M (clean table; chart 02 is right). 83M in the handoff was wrong. ARM is $ per member per month, so $1/month x 89.63M x 12 = $1,076M per year (about $1,050M on the 87.2M average members implied by Q4'24 revenue 4,517/3/17.26). The "$360M/year" was an arithmetic error in the handoff (it is not 83M x $1 x 12 = $996M, nor any other defensible figure). Break-even: a $1 rise at ARM 17.26 is offset by losing about 4.9M members (5.5%). Assumed: flat membership; modeled-free arithmetic, not a causal estimate."
Memo sections · what changedNetflix §1 lever 1, §3 decision rule. members corrected to 89.63M; $1 a month ≈ $1.08B a year; break-even ≈ 4.9M.

ML statistician answered"Pre = Q4'19-Q1'23 (14 quarters, median 3,246.5M); post = Q2'23-Q4'25 (11 quarters, median 4,322M). Median difference = 1,075.5M (findings.md 1,060M does not reproduce). Hodges-Lehmann = 1,218M (reproduces; this is what hypotheses.md reports). Both mix in the time trend and include 2025. Trend-adjusted: OLS (Ridge alpha 0.01 is ~OLS) of revenue on arm_lag1, rev_lag1, post_paid_sharing, quarter dummies, fitted on 20 training quarters Q1'20-Q4'24: post_paid_sharing = +92.4M/qtr, SE 64.1, 95% CI [-46, +231], p = 0.17. Without quarter dummies: +86.9M, SE 59.8. The model does not support a $1.2B/qtr step. (Members model: post_paid_sharing +2.23M members, SE 0.89, p = 0.022, model_card.)"

Growth-strategy partner askedcustomer_risk_scores.csv shows near-flat LOOCV predictions; chart 07 shows varying ones. Which is the selected model's out-of-sample result?
ML statistician answered"Neither file is the full story. scores.csv holds full-sample fitted values (in-sample MAE: comps 9.36, margin 1.51; Netflix 63.6M), flat because alpha = 100 shrinks the slope to ~0. The chart plots true leave-one-out predictions (leave-one-out mean reproduces its FY2021 value ~0.8-1.0; LOO MAE 10.9 and 1.7, matching the model card 11.07 and 1.79). Selected model is the same; the chart is the honest out-of-sample view. My customer_risk_scores.csv inherited the in-sample values but labels them "loocv" and "wf-CV OOF": that labelling is wrong. Only Netflix Q1'25 is a held-out score; Q2-Q4'25 were not scored."
Memo sections · what changed§2 model rows, risk 2. memo uses chart 07 and the model card for out-of-sample accuracy.
Round 1 · Q9Five Below §2Is revenue per store calculated on year-end stores or average stores? Confirm FY2022 = $2.30M.
Growth-strategy partner askedIs revenue per store calculated on year-end stores or average stores? Confirm FY2022 = $2.30M.
ML statistician answered"Revenue per store = revenue / year-end stores (data dictionary). FY2022 = $2.2958M = $2.30M. $2.60M in findings.md is wrong. On average-fleet basis FY2022 = $2.43M. Note FY2022 to FY2023-24 average is -$0.05M (-2%) per hypotheses H5; "dilution" is small."
Memo sections · what changedFive Below §2. FY2022 = $2.30M; peak-year dilution −2%.

Growth-strategy partner askedGross margin % for FY2018–FY2025. Split the FY2023→FY2024 drop (10.83% to 8.35%) and FY2024→FY2025 recovery into gross-margin and SG&A-% components, in ppt.
ML statistician answered"Identity check: gross margin - SG&A % = operating margin holds exactly for FY2018-FY2022 (residual 0.00 ppt) but NOT for FY2023-FY2025 (residual 3.67, 4.32, 4.03 ppt). So cogs_usd for FY2023+ appears to exclude a cost line that the earlier years include ... Status: OPEN, needs a check of the 10-K cost lines." "FY23->24 op margin -2.48 = gross margin -0.89, SG&A -0.94 (22.22 vs 21.28), unexplained other cost -0.65. FY24->25 +1.25 = gross margin +1.10, SG&A -0.14, other +0.29. The "other" line is the unreconciled residual; do not read it as a finding."
Memo sections · what changedFive Below open question 1, risk 8. margin bridge marked provisional and open.

You are right: 2023 and 2024 were member-led; 2022 was ARM-led. Handoff section 8 / chart-05 wording was wrong. Descriptive arithmetic, not causal."

Part D

Appendix

D1

Glossary

ARM
Average revenue per member per month: revenue ÷ average members ÷ months
UCAN
Netflix's US and Canada reporting region
Paid sharing
Netflix's 2023 policy charging for accounts used outside the household
Extra-member slot
A paid add-on that lets an outside user join an account
Net additions (net adds)
Members gained minus members lost in a quarter
Churn
Share of subscribers who cancel in a period
Break-even member loss
Member loss at which a price rise leaves revenue unchanged: x/(1+x)
Elasticity
How much demand changes when price changes
Comparable sales (comps)
Sales growth in stores open at least 15 months
Expansion rate
Net new stores ÷ prior year-end stores
Operating margin
Operating income ÷ revenue
Gross margin
(Revenue − cost of goods) ÷ revenue
SG&A
Selling, general and administrative expenses
SG&A intensity
SG&A ÷ revenue
Capex
Cash spent on stores, distribution centers and systems
Payback period
Time for a store's profit to repay its investment
Cannibalization
Sales a new store takes from nearby stores
Infill
A new store inside an existing market
Shrink
Inventory lost to theft, damage or error
Ticket
Average spend per transaction
bps
Basis points; 100 bps = 1 percentage point
ppt / percentage point
The plain difference between two percentages
XBRL
Machine-readable tags on financial filings
8-K / 10-K
SEC current-event report / SEC annual report
Leakage
When a model input already contains the answer
Ridge regression
Straight-line model with a penalty that shrinks weights to avoid overfitting
Alpha
The strength of the Ridge penalty
Overfitting
A model that memorizes noise and fails on new data
Optuna
An automated tool that searches model settings; not used here
Naive baseline
A simple guess (e.g. last value or average) a model must beat
MAE
Mean absolute error: the average size of a miss
R²
Share of variation a model explains; negative means worse than the average
Walk-forward validation
Train on past periods, predict the next, repeat
Leave-one-out validation (LOOCV)
Hold out one year, train on the rest, predict it; repeat for each year
OOF (out-of-fold)
A prediction for a row the model did not train on
In-sample fit
A prediction for a row the model trained on; flatters accuracy
Held-out test
Data kept aside and used once, at the end
Coefficient (weight)
How much a model's output moves per unit of an input
Collinearity
Two inputs moving together so a model cannot separate their effects
Momentum model
A model that mostly predicts from the previous value
Structural break
A point where the pattern in the data changes, e.g. a policy change
Spearman rho
Rank correlation from −1 to +1
p-value
Chance of a result this extreme if there were no real link
95% CI
Confidence interval: a range likely to contain the true value
Bootstrap
Re-sampling the data many times to estimate an interval
Exact permutation test
A significance test that checks every possible ordering of a small sample
Mann-Whitney test
A test of whether one group's values tend to be higher than another's
Hodges-Lehmann
A robust estimate of the median gap between two groups
OLS
Ordinary least squares: the standard straight-line fit
Uplift model
Estimates how much an action changes a person's behavior
Persuadable
A customer whose behavior an offer actually changes
Holdout
A random group that does not get a treatment, kept for comparison
Natural experiment
A real-world split that acts like random assignment
Minimum detectable effect
Smallest true effect a test can reliably detect
North Star metric
The one outcome a pilot is judged on
Guardrail metric
A metric that must not get worse during a pilot
Measured / modeled / external / assumed
The four evidence labels defined at the top
